claims.claim: The UK has no wealth tax

sources.name: PwC: United Kingdom, other taxes
sources.says: Last reviewed 23 July 2026. "Tax is not charged on an individual's wealth each year in the United Kingdom." The nil-rate band is "GBP 325,000 since 6 April 2009 and is frozen until 5 April 2031". An individual is a long-term resident if UK resident for "at least 10 of the previous 20 tax years"; only non-UK assets depend on that status. Long-term residents who leave stay in scope for up to ten years: three years for 10 to 13 years of residence, rising by one year for each further year, to a maximum of ten.

claims.claim: Since April 2025 the 4-year foreign income and gains (FIG) regime replaces non-dom status: after 10 years of non-UK residence, foreign dividends, interest and gains are untaxed for the first 4 UK tax years

sources.name: GOV.UK (HMRC): check if you can claim the 4-year foreign income and gains regime
sources.says: Published 6 April 2025. You must be in your first 4 years of UK tax residence after "at least a 10-year period as a non-UK tax resident"; "The regime is only available for a maximum period of 4 consecutive years beginning when your UK tax residency started." Eligible foreign income and gains are not taxed if you claim. Claiming means losing "tax-free allowances for Income Tax and Capital Gains Tax". The regime replaced the remittance basis on 6 April 2025.

sources.name: GOV.UK: technical note, changes to the taxation of non-UK domiciled individuals
sources.says: Updated 23 April 2024, for changes from 6 April 2025. The regime applies for the first 4 tax years "once becoming UK tax resident after a period of 10 years non-UK tax residence"; qualifying individuals "will be able to bring these funds to the UK free from any additional charges". Those who choose the regime "will lose entitlement to personal allowances and the capital gains tax annual exempt amount."

claims.note: HMRC's manual page guessed at https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/residence-and-fig-regime-manual/rfig40100 is a 404; the guidance page and the technical note carry the rule.

claims.claim: The US–UK estate and gift tax treaty gives relief

sources.name: GOV.UK (HMRC): Inheritance Tax, double taxation relief
sources.says: Last updated 6 April 2025. Lists the USA convention (11 November 1979) among six. The country of domicile or deemed domicile can tax all property; the other country generally only specified property such as immovable property there; where both still tax, the convention decides which gives credit. A long-term UK resident is treated as having deemed UK domicile. Relief is a credit capped at the overseas tax actually paid.

claims.note: HMRC's manual page IHTM27161 (https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/inheritance-tax-manual/ihtm27161, updated 7 April 2026) also lists the USA among the conventions and says its terms "must be considered and applied". Not read: the convention's own text, so how it allocates taxing rights for a US citizen who has become a long-term UK resident is not established here.

claims.claim: The UK has no retirement or passive-income visa: savings and pensions alone give no right to live there

sources.name: Taxes for Expats: retiring in the UK as an American
sources.says: Last updated August 14, 2026. "The UK does not offer a dedicated retirement visa"; pension income or savings alone give no right to live there. Routes covered: UK Ancestry (Commonwealth or related nationality, a UK-born grandparent, an intention to work; US citizenship alone does not qualify), a partner application (usually £29,000 combined income) and Skilled Worker (sponsored employment, usually at least £41,700).
